step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 11-year-old human male child presenting with progressive bulbar palsy, drooling of saliva, and respiratory failure.

evidence_items.source_quote: He had a past history of dog bite 3 months ago for which he received five doses of ARV.
Corneal smear was negative for rabies antigen.
A final diagnosis of Fazio Londe disease was made.

step10_contradiction_notes: Rabies was tested due to bulbar palsy, hypersalivation, and dog bite 3 months prior; corneal smear was negative for rabies antigen and the patient was definitively diagnosed with Fazio-Londe syndrome with full bulbar recovery on riboflavin therapy.
rationale: An 11-year-old boy presented with progressive bulbar palsy, dysphagia, continuous drooling of saliva, and respiratory failure, with a history of dog bite and 5 doses of anti-rabies vaccine 3 months prior. Corneal smear tested negative for rabies antigen, EMG and muscle biopsy showed neurogenic atrophy, and a final diagnosis of Fazio-Londe syndrome was established with marked clinical recovery on riboflavin therapy at 6 months. Rabies was explicitly tested and ruled out -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 55-year-old human man presenting with fever, altered sensorium, flaccid quadriplegia, and dysautonomia.

step4_condition_matched: Rabies (paralytic rabies in differential diagnosis, CSF PCR negative)

evidence_items.source_quote: The differential diagnosis included paralytic rabies, Cytomegalovirus (CMV), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and leptomeningeal metastases [Table 1].

CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR) panel was positive for WNV and negative for CMV, human herpes virus-6, rabies, John Cunningham virus, herpes simplex virus (HSV) 1 and 2, dengue, Japanese encephalitis (JE), nipah, chikungunya, chandipura, mumps, measles and enterovirus including poliovirus, fungi and bacteria including Myobacterium tuberculosis on day 7 (Xcyton acute encephalitis syndrome [AES], Bangalore).

step10_contradiction_notes: Initial clinical differential diagnosis included paralytic rabies due to acute flaccid quadriplegia and hypersalivation, but CSF PCR was negative for rabies and positive for West Nile virus (confirmed by WNV IgM and serum microneutralization).
rationale: A 55-year-old man presented with fever, meningoencephalitis, acute flaccid quadriplegia, and dysautonomia with hypersalivation. Paralytic rabies was considered in the initial differential diagnosis, but CSF PCR panel on day 7 tested negative for rabies and positive for West Nile virus (confirmed by serum/CSF WNV IgM ELISA and a high serum WNV neutralizing antibody titer of 40). Rabies was explicitly tested and ruled out -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 20-year-old human female (Patient K.) with limbic encephalitis and right ovarian teratoma (retrospectively characteristic of anti-NMDAR encephalitis).

step4_condition_matched: Rabies (evaluated in differential diagnosis and not confirmed)

evidence_items.source_quote: A differential diagnostic search was carried out, aimed at ruling in tuberculosis, rabies, and the use of psychotropic and narcotic drugs; none of the above was confirmed.

step10_contradiction_notes: Rabies was evaluated in the differential diagnostic workup and was not confirmed.
rationale: A 20-year-old female presented with prodromal fever followed by acute psychosis, status epilepticus, orofacial/limb hyperkinesis, and impaired swallowing, with a right ovarian teratoma (retrospectively identified as anti-NMDAR limbic encephalitis). A differential diagnostic search for tuberculosis, rabies, and psychotropic/narcotic drugs was performed and none of these was confirmed. Rabies was evaluated as a differential diagnosis and ruled out -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 76-year-old human woman returning to Canada from India with multidrug-resistant NDM-1 Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli urinary tract infection, sepsis, and toxic metabolic leukoencephalopathy.

step4_condition_matched: Rabies virus (tested negative during encephalitis workup)

evidence_items.source_quote: Test results for infectious causes of encephalitis (e.g., malaria smears, cerebrospinal fluid culture for bacteria, and staining for acid-fast bacteria and fungi) were negative, as were test results for cryptococcal antigen, herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2, Japanese encephalitis virus, and rabies virus.
Several days later, her condition worsened and she died; the final diagnosis was toxic metabolic leukoencephalopathy, probably related to sepsis.

step10_contradiction_notes: Encephalitis workup explicitly tested for rabies virus with negative results; final diagnosis was toxic metabolic leukoencephalopathy secondary to sepsis.
rationale: A 76-year-old woman returning from northern India presented with septic shock, NDM-1-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli urinary tract infection, Clostridium difficile colitis, and decreased consciousness. Diagnostic testing for infectious causes of encephalitis, including rabies virus, was explicitly negative, and the final diagnosis was toxic metabolic leukoencephalopathy related to sepsis -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 77-year-old human man presenting with Capnocytophaga canimorsus-infected arterial aneurysms 10 days after a dog bite.

step4_condition_matched: Rabies (clinically ruled out after dog bite)

evidence_items.source_quote: After 11 days, cultures of the femoral aneurysm were positive for Capnocytophaga canimorsus.
evidence_items.test_name: Femoral aneurysm tissue culture and MALDI-TOF MS

evidence_items.source_quote: The symptoms and the incubation period was not in favor for a rabies.
evidence_items.test_name: Clinical assessment of symptoms and incubation period

step10_contradiction_notes: No contradiction; Capnocytophaga canimorsus mycotic aneurysm confirmed by culture and MALDI-TOF MS, and rabies explicitly excluded.
rationale: A 77-year-old man presented with fever, asthenia, confusion, and rapidly expanding inflammatory arterial aneurysms 10 days after a dog bite on the left hand. Resected femoral aneurysm cultures were positive for Capnocytophaga canimorsus by MALDI-TOF MS, and the authors explicitly state that 'The symptoms and the incubation period was not in favor for a rabies.' Rabies was clinically ruled out -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 17-year-old Kenyan female presenting with acute psychosis, fever, orofacial dyskinesias, hypersalivation, and coma due to anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

step4_condition_matched: Rabies virus (excluded by negative PCR in blood/urine, saliva, and neck hairline skin biopsies)

evidence_items.source_quote: We immediately ran investigations comprehensive blood and/or urine tests for infection, auto-immune disease (including vasculitis) and toxic causes (including porphyria), also comprising polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for tropical fever pathogens (human immunodeficiency virus, Treponema pallidum, malaria, Leptospira, rickettsia, dengue, West Nile, chikungunya and rabies viruses - with additional testing in saliva and neck hairline skin biopsies for the latter), contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan of the head, chest and abdomen which were all normal/negative.
evidence_items.test_name: Rabies virus PCR (blood/urine, saliva, and neck hairline skin biopsies)
evidence_items.specimen: saliva and neck hairline skin biopsies

evidence_items.source_quote: On day 7 both serum and CSF autoimmune encephalitis panels returned positive for antibodies against the NMDA receptor, giving a definite diagnosis of NMDARE.
evidence_items.test_name: Serum and CSF anti-NMDA receptor antibody panel

step10_contradiction_notes: Rabies was comprehensively tested via PCR on blood/urine, saliva, and nuchal skin biopsies with negative results, and anti-NMDAR encephalitis was confirmed via serum and CSF autoantibodies.
rationale: A 17-year-old Kenyan female presented with headache, insomnia, auditory hallucinations, fever, orofacial dyskinesias, hypersalivation, and coma. PCR testing for rabies virus—including testing on saliva and neck hairline (nuchal) skin biopsies—was explicitly negative, and both serum and CSF tested positive for anti-NMDA receptor antibodies, confirming autoimmune anti-NMDAR encephalitis -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 77-year-old human female from southern Germany with fatal Borna disease virus 1 (BoDV-1) sclerosing panencephalomyelitis.

evidence_items.source_quote: Specifically, CSF samples were PCR-negative for HSV1 and HSV2-, VZV-, CMV-, Picorna viruses (enterovirus, echo-viruses, and Coxsackie viruses), EBV-DNA and tuberculosis; serologically negative for an acute infection of rickettsies, toxoplasma, Listeria, HIV, JC-virus, rabies, HSV-6, HTLV-I/II, rotavirus, norovirus, Coxsackie, and febrile seasonal meningoencephalitis (FSME); a treponema pallidum infection was serologically (TPHA-test) excluded.

A BoDV-1 infection with induced non-purulent, lymphocytic sclerosing panencephalomyelitis was diagnosed as the cause of the fatal encephalitis, both by routine immunohistopathology (we used an antibody against the phosphoprotein (P) antigen, kindly provided by Dr. D. Rubbenstroth, at a dilution of 1:3000) and real-time PCR, as previously established.
evidence_items.test_name: Brain autopsy immunohistopathology and real-time RT-PCR

step10_contradiction_notes: Rabies was serologically excluded across serial CSF/serum evaluations, and post-mortem brain immunohistopathology and RT-PCR confirmed Borna disease virus 1 (BoDV-1) panencephalomyelitis.
rationale: A 77-year-old woman in southern Germany developed rapidly progressive fatal meningoencephalitis with coma and loss of brainstem reflexes. Serial CSF and serum diagnostic panels were serologically negative for acute rabies infection, and post-mortem brain and spinal cord autopsy confirmed Borna disease virus 1 (BoDV-1) sclerosing panencephalomyelitis via immunohistopathology, Joest-Degen inclusion bodies, and real-time RT-PCR -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 22-year-old human man presenting with involuntary jaw movements, dysphagia, limb tremors, hypertonia, and myospasm.

evidence_items.source_quote: Considering his medical history, rabies and tetanus antibody tests were performed, which turned out to be negative.
The results were negative in the serum and CSF, except for anti-GlyR antibodies at a titer of 1:3.2 in the CSF.
evidence_items.test_name: Cell-based indirect immunofluorescence autoimmune encephalitis panel

step10_contradiction_notes: Rabies antibody testing was negative, and CSF anti-GlyR antibodies confirmed progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM) with complete recovery (mRS 0) after immunotherapy.
rationale: A 22-year-old man presented with prodromal vomiting, fever, and diarrhea followed by involuntary jaw movements, dysphagia, limb tremors, and increased muscle tone. Rabies and tetanus antibody tests were performed and were negative; CSF tested positive for anti-glycine receptor (anti-GlyR) antibodies (1:3.2), establishing a diagnosis of anti-GlyR antibody-related PERM with full recovery after methylprednisolone, IVIG, and plasma exchange -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 46-year-old Japanese man presenting with generalized tetanus (trismus, risus sardonicus, neck stiffness) 19 days after a bite from a rabies-immunized pet dog.

step4_condition_matched: Rabies (considered in differential diagnosis after dog bite and clinically/epidemiologically ruled out)

evidence_items.source_quote: He was asked by a friend to look after a pet canine with rabies immunization for a couple of days.
evidence_items.test_name: Animal exposure and source animal vaccination history

evidence_items.source_quote: The differential diagnoses were tetany due to hypocalcemia, rabies, or Strychnine poisoning. These differential diagnoses were ruled out because the serum calcium levels were normal (9.0 mg/dL, normal range: 8.8-10.1 mg/dL); the patient did not have symptoms specific to rabies, such as mydriasis, increased salivation, and hydrophobia; and there was no definite history of poisoning.
The canine that bit his hand did not show any signs of illness for 4 weeks during the period in which it was kept in his care. Therefore, we thought it unlikely that the canine had tetanus or rabies.

step10_contradiction_notes: Rabies was considered in the differential diagnosis of trismus/spasms following a dog bite and was explicitly ruled out based on absence of rabies-specific symptoms (no hydrophobia, hypersalivation, or mydriasis), prior rabies vaccination and 4-week healthy observation of the biting dog, Japan's rabies-free status, and complete recovery with tetanus treatment.
rationale: A 46-year-old Japanese man developed trismus, laughter spasms, and neck stiffness 3 weeks after a bite from a rabies-immunized pet dog. Rabies was included in the differential diagnosis and explicitly ruled out based on the absence of hydrophobia, hypersalivation, and mydriasis, the biting dog's rabies immunization and healthy status over 4 weeks of observation, and the patient's rapid recovery with human tetanus immunoglobulin and metronidazole for generalized tetanus -> NEGATIVE.
